input: The selectivity values reported for the benchmark material differ markedly between the two groups, and the difference is large enough that it cannot be dismissed as routine scatter between laboratories. Both groups studied the same material class, yet the conditions under which their measurements and calculations were carried out were not equivalent, and this lack of equivalence is central to how the disagreement should be read. One set of results rests on single-component measurements combined with IAST calculations, whereas the other rests on measurements made with gas mixtures, in which the components compete for the same adsorption sites. Mixture behaviour is, arguably, the more demanding test, because competition between components is present in the measurement itself rather than introduced afterwards through a model. At the same time, mixture measurements are harder to control, and small differences in feed composition or in the approach to equilibrium can shift the reported values in ways that are difficult to trace afterwards. On balance, a limited preference for the mixture-based values seems reasonable, although the preference is by no means unconditional. It holds only where the mixture measurements were made at compositions close to the separation task of interest and where equilibrium was demonstrated rather than assumed, and it should not be extended beyond those conditions without further evidence.

The other group measured gas mixtures directly, with the components competing for the same adsorption sites. Mixture measurement is the more demanding test: competition is present in the measurement itself, not added afterwards through a model. Mixture measurements are also harder to control. Small differences in feed composition or in the approach to equilibrium can shift the reported values, and the shift is difficult to trace afterwards. Single-component data remain useful for screening materials before mixture tests are run. Reported values from either route carry the conditions of their measurement with them. A limited preference for the mixture-based values rests on two conditions. The mixture measurements must use compositions close to the separation task of interest, and equilibrium must be demonstrated, not assumed. Outside those conditions, the preference does not extend.
